messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 77

At thirty-four, Elias moves through his days with the careful, measured steps of someone walking on ice. The Tuesday it happens is bright and ordinary. He is backing his department van toward the loading dock, adjusting the rearview mirror, when he misses the paraprofessional cutting across the blind spot. The impact sounds like a heavy door slamming on hardwood. When he stumbles out, the air leaves his lungs. Her leg is bent at a wrong angle, glass and asphalt surrounding her. His own hands tremble so violently he drops his keys. Sirens wail. He sits on the curb, staring at his palms, waiting for the arrest that never comes, only the quiet, suffocating realization that he broke her. Months later, the memory does not fade; it colonizes him. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. to the phantom sound of crushing metal, his heart hammering against his ribs. He lies rigid, listening to his wife’s steady breathing, calculating how fast she would have to run if he suddenly bolted from bed. He stops driving. He takes the bus, then walks two miles to his middle school, even in rain, because the smell of hot rubber and exhaust triggers a dry heave. At work, he avoids the parking lot entirely, slipping through the staff entrance like an intruder. His office door stays shut. He used to spend hours on the playground during lunch, sitting on the mulch, watching kids chase each other. Now he monitors the security feed from his desk, squinting at the grainy video until his eyes burn, convinced that if he looks away for a second, another life will shatter. The guilt is a physical weight. He tells himself he does not deserve to be a school counselor. He mentors teenagers who talk about college, about careers, about the future, and each word feels like a judgment. When a student trips in the hallway and scrapes their knee, Elias flinches so hard he knocks his coffee mug off the desk. He apologizes to the floor. He cancels staff meetings, telling himself he is “too busy,” when the truth is he cannot bear the sound of a hard-soled shoe on tile. At home, he sleeps on the edge of the mattress, one arm dangling off, ready to spring up at the first car backfire down the street. His wife packs his lunch, handles the mortgage, speaks for him when visitors come to the door. He watches her exhaustion and wants to pull her close, but his body remains coiled, braced against an invisible impact that never stops repeating in his head. He goes to work. He opens the blinds. He grades crisis referral forms with meticulous care, underlining every safety protocol twice, triple-checking the emergency evacuation routes as if precision might undo what already happened. On Fridays, he walks to the faculty lot at dusk, alone, and presses his forehead against the cold passenger window of his abandoned van. He does not get in. He just stands there, breathing through the tightness in his chest, waiting for the world to stop moving just long enough to let him forgive himself.
